meaning: “Unless A happens first, B can't happen.” The second half is usually negative.
connection: Verb nai-form／い-adj. くない／noun・な-adj. でない + ことには

senses.label: Unless ... first, can't ...
senses.meaning: A is a necessary condition for B. Without A, B is out of the question. The second half must be negative. It stresses a “prerequisite” more strongly than 「〜なければ」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ことには + 〜ない／分からない／始まらない／何とも言えない
examples: I won't know if it's any good until I actually try it.
Unless the president gives approval, we can't move the plan forward.
I can't say anything until I meet the person myself.

senses.label: With adjectives and nouns
senses.meaning: With adjectives or nouns, it means “unless something is in a certain state, it won't work”. い-adjectives take 「〜くないことには」. Nouns and な-adjectives take 「〜でないことには」.
senses.connection: い-adj. くない／noun・な-adj. でない + ことには
examples: Unless you're physically strong, you can't keep doing this job.
Unless the price comes down a bit, it probably won't sell well.

notes: The second half must be a negative result (「分からない」「始まらない」「進まない」). It cannot take an intention, a request or a positive result. ✕「実際に見ないことには、買いましょう」→○「実際に見ないことには、買うかどうか決められない」.

It differs by only a few kana from 「〜ないことはない」 but means something completely different: 「食べてみないことには分からない」 is “I can't know until I try it”, while 「食べないことはない」 is “it's not that I don't eat it”. Check whether it is 「ことには」 or 「ことはない」, or you will get the whole sentence backwards.
The first half must be in the negative form. Don't write an affirmative just because the English says “only after ...”. ✕「使ってみることには、分からない」→○「使ってみないことには、分からない」.
The contracted 「〜ないことにゃ」 is very casual and only for close friends. To a boss or client, say 「〜ないことには、何とも申し上げられません」.

daily.title: Unsure about clothes online
daily.description: A friend recommends some clothes, and you say you need to try them on first.
daily.example: I can't tell if the size fits until I try it on.

daily.title: Planning what to pack
daily.description: You talk with family about what to bring and say you need the forecast first.
daily.example: I can't decide what to take until I check the weather forecast.

daily.title: Learning a language
daily.description: You share your experience of learning to speak a language.
daily.example: Unless you speak every day, your conversation skills won't improve.

work.title: Holding off in a meeting
work.description: The person in charge says they can't judge without full data.
work.example: We can't make a decision until we have detailed data.

work.title: Replying to a client
work.description: You say you must first check the other company's intentions.
work.example: We are unable to reply until we confirm your company's intentions.

etymology: Negative 「ない」 + the formal noun 「こと」 + 「には」 (marking a situation). Literally “in the situation of not doing ...”. It became fixed as “unless ... first”.

similar.title: 〜ないと (if not ...)
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning. 「〜ないと」 is the everyday spoken negative condition; anything can follow it, and it can take 「いけない」 to express obligation. 「〜ないことには」 stresses that “if the prerequisite isn't met, nothing can start”, is limited to negative results, and sounds more formal.

similar.title: 〜てからでないと
similar.explanation: Also means “can't ... unless ... first”, but it focuses on time order (「確認してからでないと、送れない」: confirm first, then send). 「〜ないことには」 focuses on whether the condition itself is met, with no necessary order in time.

similar.title: 〜なくして（は）
similar.explanation: A written-style N1 pattern that attaches to nouns and means “without ..., there is no ...” (「努力なくして成功はない」). 「〜ないことには」 mainly attaches to the negative form of verbs and is common in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜なしに（は）／〜なしでは
similar.explanation: Attaches to nouns and means “without ..., ...” (「許可なしには入れない」). The meaning is close, but 「なしには」 looks at the lack of a thing, while 「〜ないことには」 looks at not having done an action or not being in a certain state first.

formation: Built from the negative 「ない」, the formal noun 「こと」, the case particle 「に」 and the topic particle 「は」. 「ないこと」 sums up “not having done something” as a state, 「に」 means “in that state”, and 「は」 singles it out as the point at issue. Literally it says “in the state where ... hasn't been done yet, (things are ...)”, and the natural conclusion is “then it won't work out”, which is why the second half is always negative. Because the whole pattern describes a state where a prerequisite is missing, the 「ない」 in the first half can never be dropped; and because it spotlights that prerequisite, it sounds more like a “precondition” than the plain 「〜なければ」.

meaning: A strong wish for something hard to achieve: “Isn't there some way to ...?”, “If only ...”.
connection: Verb nai-form (usually potential) + ものか／ものだろうか／ものでしょうか

senses.label: Strong wish
senses.meaning: It looks like a question, but it expresses a strong wish for something difficult: “Is there any way to ...?” Often used with 「何とか」, 「どうにか」, or 「もう少し」. Mostly said to oneself or thought privately.
senses.connection: Potential verb nai-form／ならない + ものか (+ と思う・と考える)
examples: Isn't there some way I can help him?
Can't something be done about this traffic jam?
I'm wondering if there's a way to travel a little more cheaply.

senses.label: Polite inquiry
senses.meaning: 「〜ないものだろうか」 and 「〜ないものでしょうか」 sound softer. They are used to politely express a hope and ask whether it might be possible.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ものだろうか／ものでしょうか (often with 「〜てもらえない」 or 「〜ていただけない」)
examples: Would it be possible to extend the deadline by one more day?
Isn't there anyone who can solve this problem?

notes: Although the form is 「ない＋か」, it expresses “I really wish I could ...”, not a negative question or a rebuke. 「何とか彼を助けられないものか」 means “I wish I could somehow save him”; if you read it as “can't you save him?”, you get the speaker's stance wrong.

The direction is exactly opposite to 「〜ものか」: 「負けるものか」 (affirmative form) means “I won't lose, no way”, while 「勝てないものか」 (negative form) means “I wish I could win”. Whether the preceding form is affirmative or negative decides whether it means “no way” or “I wish”.

When talking about whether you yourself can do something, use the potential form: ✕「何とか休みを取らないものか」→○「何とか休みを取れないものか」. The question is “is it possible?”, so it is mostly used with 「〜られない」「〜できない」「ならない」「もらえない」.

When asking a boss or client directly, 「〜ていただけないものでしょうか」 is appropriate. Saying 「〜てくれないものか」 sounds like muttering a complaint to yourself, and said to someone's face it comes across as resentful and rude.

daily.title: Trouble sleeping
daily.description: Someone who can't sleep well mutters to themselves.
daily.example: If only I could sleep soundly every night.

daily.title: Wanting a pet
daily.description: A child living in an apartment grumbles to the family.
daily.example: I wish we could have a cat at our place too.

daily.title: Reading an opinion column
daily.description: An editorial or essay expresses the writer's wish.
daily.example: Isn't there some way to put an end to conflict?

work.title: Asking the boss for budget
work.description: A staff member politely asks the boss for more budget.
work.example: Would it be possible to increase the budget a little more?

work.title: Improving operations
work.description: In a meeting, you explain why you're considering a new system.
work.example: We're looking at a new system, hoping to find a way to work more efficiently.

etymology: Negative 「ない」 + the formal noun 「もの」 + the question particle 「か」. 「ものか」 originally expressed a strong or rhetorical question. After a negative, the rhetorical “Can't it be ...?” gradually turned into a wish: “If only ...”.

similar.title: 〜ないかな (wish)
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; both express a wish through a negative question. 「〜ないかな」 is relaxed spoken language (「早くバス来ないかな」), and what you wish for need not be difficult. 「〜ないものか」 is stronger and more bookish, usually refers to something hard to achieve that calls for some effort, and often goes with 「何とか」「どうにか」.

similar.title: 〜たいものだ・〜てほしいものだ
similar.explanation: Also built on 「もの」 and also expresses a strong wish, but states “I really want to ...” directly as a statement (「一度行ってみたいものだ」). 「〜ないものか」 uses a question form and carries a feeling of searching for a way and a touch of anxiety.

similar.title: 〜ものか・〜もんか
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are built from 「もの＋か」. 「ものか」 attaches to the affirmative form and is a rhetorical “how could ...?” expressing strong denial (「あんな店、二度と行くものか」). Once it attaches to the negative as 「ないものか」, the rhetorical “can't it be ...?” turns into a wish.

formation: Built from the negative 「ない」, the formal noun 「もの」, and the question particle 「か」. 「ものか」 is originally a rhetorical question charged with strong emotion, so 「〜ないものか」 literally asks “is it really (not) possible to ...?”. The speaker is pressing “isn't there any way?”, and behind it lies the feeling “I really wish there were”, so the rhetorical question turns into a wish. The first half is often in the potential form precisely because the question is “can it be done or not?”. Adding 「だろう」 or 「でしょう」 turns the assertive rhetorical question into a tentative one, which softens the tone into a polite request or inquiry.

meaning: “On the occasion of ...”: at the start of (or while preparing for) something important. Formal and written.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + にあたって・にあたり・にあたっての + noun

senses.label: On the occasion of
senses.meaning: Used when starting something important or special. Common in speeches, notices, and documents. 「にあたり」 is more written than 「にあたって」.
senses.connection: Noun (開始・出発・就任・入学, etc.)／verb dictionary form + にあたって／にあたり、／にあたっての + noun
examples: As the new year began, I set my goals for the year.
To open this meeting, allow me to say a few words.
We've put together some points to note when studying abroad.

senses.label: When undertaking ...
senses.meaning: Shows what you need to keep in mind or prepare when taking on a task. The second half is usually “must ...”, “should ...”, or “please ...”.
senses.connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + にあたっては
examples: When renting an apartment, you need to read the contract carefully.
When conducting the survey, please take great care with personal information.

notes: Use it only for the start of an important, one-time formal event (opening a business, taking office, entering school, signing a contract). Used for everyday trivia it sounds comical: ✕「昼ご飯を食べるにあたって」→○「昼ご飯を食べる前に」.
The second half is an active act made for the occasion, such as preparation, resolve or a speech. It cannot take something that merely happens: ✕「出発にあたって、雨が降り出した」→○「出発しようとしたら、雨が降り出した」.

Don't confuse it with the full verb 「当たる」: 「ボールが頭に当たって痛い」 (to hit) and 「宝くじに当たって」 (to win a lottery) are not this pattern. It is “on the occasion of ...” only when the first part is a moment or an event.
Formal speeches often open with 「〜にあたりまして、一言ご挨拶申し上げます」. In written notices to clients or superiors, 「〜にあたり、〜をお願いいたします」 is more appropriate than the spoken 「〜とき」.

daily.title: Reading an admission guide
daily.description: You see it in the school's admission handbook.
daily.example: Please prepare the required documents for admission.

daily.title: Visiting before marriage
daily.description: You tell a friend how you prepared for your wedding.
daily.example: Before getting married, we went to greet our parents.

work.title: Opening a new shop
work.description: The owner thanks guests at the opening ceremony.
work.example: On the occasion of today's opening, I offer my heartfelt thanks.

work.title: Internal notice
work.description: A notice from General Affairs to all staff.
work.example: We will hold a briefing on the introduction of the new system.

work.title: Inaugural speech
work.description: The new president speaks at an all-staff meeting.
work.example: On taking office as president, allow me to share my aspirations.

etymology: 「あたる（当たる）」 originally means “to hit, to face directly”. It extended to “to face (a moment)”. 「〜にあたって」 means “right at this moment of ...”, so it became a written way to say “on the occasion of”.

similar.title: 〜に際して
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning; both are formal and written, and in most cases they are interchangeable. 「に際して」 is more objective, stressing “right at that moment”; 「にあたって」 carries more of the feel of “actively preparing and resolving for an important event about to begin”.

similar.title: 〜際（に）
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning (“when ...”), but it can be used for ordinary matters (「お降りの際は、足元にご注意ください」). 「にあたって」 is only for important, special occasions, and the second half is mostly preparation or resolve.

similar.title: 〜に先立って
similar.explanation: Both are used at the start of an important matter. 「に先立って」 clearly means “before ... (do something first)”; 「にあたって」 covers both the time before and the moment itself, with the focus on “facing this moment”.

similar.title: 〜に当たる
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are built from the verb 「当たる」. 「〜に当たる」 means “to correspond to, to fall on” (「今日は父の命日に当たる」) and expresses a correspondence; 「〜にあたって」 means “on the occasion of facing ...” and is followed by an action taken for it.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」 plus the て-form of the verb 「当たる」 (or its continuative form 「当たり」). 「当たる」 originally means “to face squarely, to run into”, so 「Nに当たる」 means “to meet the moment of N head-on”. When people face an important event, they naturally prepare and resolve to do something, so the second half is mostly “we must ...”, “please ...”, or a speech. The て-form 「当たって」 sets that moment as the backdrop to what follows, and the continuative 「当たり」 is a written pause, hence more formal. Because “facing it squarely” also implies actively confronting the occasion, it carries a bit more sense of positive preparation than 「に際して」.

meaning: B changes or adjusts according to differences or changes in A.
connection: Noun + に応じて・に応じ・に応じた + noun

senses.label: According to
senses.meaning: B changes to match A. A is usually a noun that varies or changes: 「能力」, 「年齢」, 「状況」, 「希望」, 「収入」.
senses.connection: Noun + に応じて／に応じ、
examples: The amount of tax changes according to income.
We change the menu according to the season.
Keep doing exercise that suits your stamina, without overdoing it.

senses.label: Matching ...
senses.meaning: 「に応じた + noun」 modifies a noun: “suited to ...”, “in proportion to ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + に応じた + noun
examples: We pay a salary based on experience.
Teaching tailored to each person's level is important.

senses.label: Respond to / accept
senses.meaning: As a verb, 「〜に応じる」 means to accept or respond to a request, invitation, interview, etc.
senses.connection: Noun (要求・依頼・注文・取材・誘い, etc.) + に応じる／に応じて
examples: The company agreed to the union's demands.
He agreed to the reporter's interview and talked about the incident.

notes: The first part must be something that varies in degree or changes (「収入」「年齢」「状況」「希望」), and the second half changes accordingly. It can't be used when the first part is a single fixed event: ✕「会議に応じて資料を準備する」→○「会議に合わせて資料を準備する」.
「応じる（おうじる）」 and 「応える（こたえる）」 share a kanji but differ in meaning: 「要求に応じる」 is “to agree to a demand”, while 「期待に応える」 is “to live up to expectations”. ✕「期待に応じる」→○「期待に応える」.
The negatives in Sense 3, 「取材に応じない」 and 「交渉に応じない」, mean “refuse an interview, refuse to negotiate”. They are very common in news; don't read them as “not according to ...”.

daily.title: At the gym
daily.description: A trainer explains the program to a new member.
daily.example: Let's plan your workout based on your age and fitness.

daily.title: Ordering a set meal
daily.description: A server tells a customer the rice portion can be adjusted.
daily.example: You can adjust the amount of rice to your liking.

daily.title: Reading a job ad
daily.description: You read it while browsing part-time job listings.
daily.example: The hourly wage depends on experience.

work.title: Proposal to a client
work.description: A salesperson presents options to a client.
work.example: We'll propose a plan that fits your budget.

work.title: Explaining HR policy
work.description: HR explains the bonus system.
work.example: Bonuses are paid according to performance.

etymology: 「応じる」 is a サ-irregular verb made of the kanji 「応」 + 「じる（ずる）」. It originally means “to respond, to answer”. From “responding to someone” it extended to “changing in line with ...”.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; it can also express “differs depending on ...” (「人によって考え方が違う」) and stresses that differences objectively exist. 「に応じて」 stresses actively adjusting to different situations.

similar.title: 〜に合わせて・〜に合った
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning. 「に合わせて」 stresses “bringing something into line with, matching” (「音楽に合わせて踊る」), and its first part can be a single fixed thing; 「に応じて」 stresses changing according to degree or circumstances.

similar.title: 〜次第だ・〜次第で (depends on)
similar.explanation: Both say that the second half is decided by the first. 「次第で」 stresses “it all depends on ...”, with the outcome determined by the first part (「天気次第で中止する」); 「に応じて」 stresses adjusting proportionally or according to the situation.

similar.title: 〜にこたえて
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; both have the sense of “responding to the other party”, and both are written with 「応」. 「に応えて」 means satisfying the other's expectations or demands (「期待に応えて優勝した」); 「に応じて」 means complying with or accepting the other's request, or changing according to circumstances.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」 plus the て-form of the する-verb 「応じる（応ずる）」. 「応」 means “to respond, to correspond”, and 「応じる」 means “to react appropriately to something”. 「Nに応じて」 means “reacting to the circumstances of N”: when N changes, the second half changes with it, which is where “changing in accordance with ...” comes from, so the first part must be something that varies. When N is the other party's request or invitation, “responding” becomes “accepting, agreeing”, which is Sense 3. 「に応じた＋noun」 turns “corresponding” into a modifier.

meaning: Affects or concerns something serious (life, reputation, etc.), or is involved in something.
connection: Noun + にかかわる／にかかわって／にかかわった

senses.label: Affects (seriously)
senses.meaning: Has a major impact on something important. A is usually 「命」, 「名誉」, 「信用」, 「将来」, 「健康」, etc. The tone is serious; 「命にかかわる」 (life-threatening) is very common.
senses.connection: Noun + にかかわる (+ 問題・病気, etc.)
examples: This is a serious, life-or-death problem.
A mistake like that would damage the company's credibility.

senses.label: Be involved in
senses.meaning: Being part of some work or connected to something. A neutral “related to, involved in”.
senses.connection: Noun + にかかわる／にかかわって／にかかわった + noun
examples: I've worked in education for many years.
A person involved in the incident was arrested.
He's involved in making the movie.

notes: It differs from 「〜にかかわらず」 and 「〜にもかかわらず」 only in the ending, but the meanings are completely different: 「命にかかわる」 is “life-threatening”, 「天候にかかわらず」 is “regardless of the weather”, and 「雨にもかかわらず」 is “despite the rain”.
Sense 1 (affect) is very strong and used only for weighty matters such as life, reputation, credibility and one's future. Used for trifles it sounds exaggerated: ✕「この遅れは昼休みにかかわる」→○「この遅れで昼休みが短くなる」.
「関わる」 and 「関する」 look alike but differ: 「教育に関する本」 is “a book about education” (a topic), while 「教育に関わる仕事」 is “work involved in education” (actual participation).

daily.title: Urging a family member to see a doctor
daily.description: Family persuade someone who doesn't want to go to the hospital.
daily.example: If you leave that illness alone, it could be life-threatening.

daily.title: Talking about future dreams
daily.description: A student talks with a friend about the job they want.
daily.example: In the future, I want a job working with children.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: You see a report about a personal data leak.
daily.example: Information related to privacy was leaked.

work.title: Quality meeting
work.description: The boss asks for a quality issue to be handled right away.
work.example: This issue affects quality, so please deal with it immediately.

work.title: Job interview
work.description: A candidate describes their past work.
work.example: Since joining the company, I've been involved in developing new products.

etymology: 「かかわる」 was 「かかはる」 in old Japanese, meaning “to be tied to, to be caught up in”. The kanji 「関」 and 「係」 were borrowed for “connection”. From “being connected”, it came to mean “having a serious impact on ...”.

similar.title: 〜に関して・〜に関する
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; both can be translated “related to ...”. 「に関して」 only gives the topic, “about ...” (「環境に関して話す」); 「にかかわる」 expresses actual involvement, connection or serious impact, and is stronger.

similar.title: 〜にまつわる
similar.explanation: An N1 pattern with a similar meaning, “related to ..., concerning ...”, mostly modifying legends, stories and anecdotes (「この寺にまつわる伝説」). 「にかかわる」 is more widely usable and can express involvement or a serious impact.

similar.title: 〜にかかわらず
similar.explanation: Same origin: it is built from 「かかわらず」, the negative classical form of 「かかわる」, which literally means “not related to ...”, hence “regardless of ...” (「年齢にかかわらず参加できる」). It shares the root with 「にかかわる」; one says “related”, the other “unrelated”, which makes the pair easiest to mix up if you don't compare them.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」 plus the verb 「かかわる（関わる）」. 「かかわる」 originally means “to be tied up with, to be connected to”. When a person actively gets involved with something, that is “to take part in” (Sense 2); when a matter is tied to something as vital as life or reputation, it means it may be damaged, i.e. “to affect, to jeopardize” (Sense 1), which is why Sense 1 often has a serious, negative tone. As a modifier, 「〜に関わる＋noun」 attaches directly to the noun, as in 「命に関わる病気」.

meaning: The success or outcome depends entirely on A: “it all comes down to ...”.
connection: Noun／〜かどうか／question word ... か + にかかっている

senses.label: Depends on
senses.meaning: The result is decided entirely by A. Common pattern: 「AはBにかかっている」. The subject is often 「成功」, 「結果」, 「将来」, 「勝敗」. A is often 「努力」, 「やる気」, or a 「〜かどうか」 clause.
senses.connection: Noun／〜かどうか／question word ... か + にかかっている／にかかっています
examples: Whether we win the game depends on the players' efforts.
This company's future depends on whether the new product sells.
In the end, it all comes down to the person's own motivation.

senses.label: Rests on someone's shoulders
senses.meaning: 「〜の肩にかかっている」 or 「〜の双肩にかかっている」 means a heavy responsibility rests on someone; everything depends on them.
senses.connection: Person + の肩／の双肩 + にかかっている
examples: The team's fate rests on the captain's shoulders.
The whole family's livelihood rests on his shoulders.

notes: The subject is a “result, success or failure, or future”, and the first part is the factor that decides it. Reverse them and the meaning is wrong: ✕「努力は合格にかかっている」→○「合格は努力にかかっている」.
When the first part is a clause, nominalize it with 「〜かどうか」 or “question word ... か”: ✕「成功するにかかっている」→○「成功するかどうかにかかっている」.

Distinguish it from other senses of 「かかる」: 「壁に絵がかかっている」 (hanging), 「医者にかかっている」 (seeing a doctor) and 「エンジンがかかっている」 (the engine is running) are not this pattern. Only “result ＋は＋ factor ＋にかかっている” means “depends on”.

daily.title: Encouraging a child before exams
daily.description: A parent talks to a child preparing for exams.
daily.example: Whether you pass or not depends on how hard you work.

daily.title: Planning a weekend barbecue
daily.description: Friends are worried about the weather.
daily.example: Whether we can have the barbecue tomorrow depends on the weather.

daily.title: Reading sports news
daily.description: You see it in a report about the finals.
daily.example: The championship depends on the result of the final match.

work.title: Project kickoff
work.description: A project manager speaks to the team.
work.example: The success of this project depends on everyone's cooperation.

work.title: Management meeting
work.description: The president analyzes this term's results.
work.example: This term's results depend on whether the new product becomes a hit.

etymology: 「かかる（掛かる）」 originally means “to hang, to be hung on ...”. From the image of something hanging on one support point, it came to mean “to rest entirely on ...”, “to depend on ...”.

similar.title: 〜次第だ・〜次第で (depends on)
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning and interchangeable. 「次第」 attaches directly to a noun and is more colloquial (「やる気次第だ」); 「にかかっている」 carries the image of “a burden hanging on ...”, stresses that the result is entirely governed by the first part, and sounds more formal.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: It can also mean “depends on ...” (「天候によって中止する」), but it stresses “differs according to circumstances”; 「にかかっている」 stresses that success or failure, the result, rests entirely on this one factor.

similar.title: 〜にかかったら／〜にかかっては
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are built from 「かかる」 and both mean “to fall on ...”. 「にかかったら」 means “once it's in someone's hands (...)” (「彼にかかったら、どんな機械もすぐ直る」), and the second half is either easy handling or helplessness; 「にかかっている」 means a result depends on some factor.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」, the て-form of the verb 「かかる（掛かる）」, and 「いる」. 「かかる」 originally means “to hang on”, so 「AはBにかかっている」 literally says “A hangs on B”. Whether something stays up depends entirely on the hook it hangs from, which extends to “A's success rests entirely on B”. 「ている」 expresses that this “hanging” state continues, so this pattern is almost always used in the 「ている」 form. 「〜の肩にかかっている」 is the same image made concrete: a heavy burden hangs on someone's shoulders, and everything depends on that person.

meaning: “When it comes to ... (no one can beat them)”. Used to praise someone's skill in a field or to express confidence.
connection: Noun + にかけては／にかけても

senses.label: Best at ...
senses.meaning: Someone is the best in a field or skill; no one can match them. The second half is usually positive: 「誰にも負けない」, 「右に出る者はいない」, 「自信がある」, 「一番だ」.
senses.connection: Noun (skill・field) + にかけては
examples: When it comes to cooking, no one can beat my mom.
When it comes to running fast, he's the best in the class.
When it comes to math, I'm confident I can beat anyone.

senses.label: Also good at ...
senses.meaning: 「にかけても」 means “also (just as good) when it comes to ...”. Used to add another strength on top of one already mentioned.
senses.connection: Noun + にかけても
examples: He's a great singer, and he dances at a professional level too.

notes: Use it only for abilities, skills, knowledge and other strong points, with high praise in the second half. Used for a flaw it becomes sarcasm: 「遅刻にかけては彼の右に出る者はいない」 mocks “he's the best at being late”.
Said about yourself, it sounds extremely confident; saying 「〜にかけては誰にも負けません」 to a boss or client can come across as arrogant. In interviews and the like, 「〜には自信があります」 is safer.
Don't confuse it with 「〜から〜にかけて」, which expresses a range: 「夜から朝にかけては雨が降る」 means “from night into morning”. Although 「は」 follows, it does not mean “in the area of ...”.

daily.title: Talking about siblings
daily.description: You mention your younger brother's gaming skills.
daily.example: When it comes to video games, I'm no match for my little brother.

daily.title: Introducing your strengths
daily.description: You introduce yourself to the class at the start of term.
daily.example: When it comes to getting up early, I'm confident.

daily.title: Reading sports news
daily.description: A report praises an athlete.
daily.example: When it comes to speed, no player can top him.

work.title: Recommending staff
work.description: A department head recommends a team member to a director.
work.example: When it comes to negotiation skills, she's the best in the company.

work.title: Company pitch
work.description: Presenting your company's strengths to a client.
work.example: When it comes to quality, we're confident we can beat any other company.

etymology: 「かける（掛ける）」 can mean “to stake, to bet” (as in 「命をかける」). One theory: 「〜にかけては」 came from “staking everything on this point” and became “as far as ... goes (the best)”.

similar.title: 〜点で・〜という点では
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; both mean “in terms of ...”. 「〜点で」 neutrally specifies the angle of evaluation and can be used for good or bad (「値段の点で不満がある」); 「にかけては」 is used only to praise outstanding ability, and the second half is often 「誰にも負けない」「右に出る者はいない」.

similar.title: 〜こととなると／〜ことになると (when it comes to)
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; it also singles out one field. 「〜のこととなると」 stresses “once the topic comes up, one's attitude and behavior differ from usual” (「釣りのこととなると夢中になる」); 「にかけては」 stresses being the best in that field.

similar.title: 〜から〜にかけて
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are built from the verb 「かける」. 「から〜にかけて」 expresses a range of time or space, “from ... to ... or so” (「関東から東北にかけて」); 「にかけては」 means “in terms of ... (the most outstanding)”. The two differ in meaning and are told apart by 「から」 and the content of the second half.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」, the て-form of the verb 「かける（掛ける）」, and the topic particle 「は」. 「かける」 has the sense of “to stake, to put up” (「命をかける」「名誉にかけて誓う」). One way to understand 「Nにかけては」 is “as far as N, on which one would stake everything, is concerned”: being willing to stake everything on one field shows complete confidence in it, so the second half is always “nobody can beat ...” or “very confident”. 「は」 singles the field out for contrast, hinting “I can't speak for the rest, but in this area ...”; with 「も」 it would mean “in this area too ...”.

meaning: Adds B on top of A: “in addition to ...”, “not only ... but also ...”.
connection: Noun + に加えて・に加え

senses.label: In addition to
senses.meaning: Adds another thing of the same kind on top of something. Mostly used in writing, news, and formal settings. The second half often has 「〜も」.
senses.connection: Noun + に加えて／に加え、
examples: On top of the rain, the wind is getting stronger.
This job requires Chinese in addition to English.
On top of rising prices, even our salaries went down.

senses.label: With verbs and clauses
senses.meaning: With verbs or adjectives, first turn them into nouns with 「こと」 or 「の」, then add 「に加えて」.
senses.connection: Verb・adjective plain form + こと／の + に加えて
examples: Not only is he good at his job, he's also a nice person.
It's far from the station, and on top of that the rent is high.

notes: The two parts must point in the same direction (both good or both bad). It can't be used when one is good and the other bad: ✕「値段が安いのに加えて、品質が悪い」→○「値段は安いが、品質が悪い」.
When it follows a verb or adjective, you must nominalize first: ✕「駅から遠いに加えて、家賃も高い」→○「駅から遠いことに加えて、家賃も高い」.

The 「の」 in 「〜のに加えて」 is a nominalizer; don't confuse it with the concessive 「のに」 (“even though”): 「安いのに加えて」 means “it's cheap, and on top of that ...”, while 「安いのに」 means “even though it's cheap, ...”.

daily.title: Complaining about the rainy season
daily.description: Complaining about the weather with a friend in summer.
daily.example: It's not just hot, it's terribly humid too.

daily.title: Watching the weather forecast
daily.description: A TV forecast gives a warning.
daily.example: Along with heavy rain, watch out for lightning too.

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Recommending your favorite place to a friend.
daily.example: This place has great food, and the service is good too.

work.title: Job posting
work.description: Requirements in a company's job ad.
work.example: We're looking for people with English skills in addition to work experience.

work.title: Explaining a price increase
work.description: Explaining the reasons for raising prices to a client.
work.example: In addition to labor costs, raw material costs are also rising.

etymology: 「加える（くわえる）」 means “to add”. 「〜に加えて」 literally means “adding on top of ...”, so it became a written expression for adding things up.

similar.title: 〜上(に)
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; it also expresses addition, but attaches directly to the plain form of verbs and adjectives (「安い上においしい」) and carries a subjective evaluation. 「に加えて」 mainly attaches to nouns and is written and objective, common in news and reports.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; common in both speech and writing, and attaches directly to all kinds of words (「安いだけでなく、おいしい」). 「に加えて」 is more written and stresses “adding one more item on top”.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning but more written and stiffer, meaning “not only ... but also ...”; it often pairs with 「も」 or 「まで」 and stresses a widening range. 「に加えて」 stresses piling up things of the same kind.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」 plus the て-form of the verb 「加える（添加）」. 「Aに加える」 originally means “to add to A” (「スープに塩を加える」). Once grammaticalized, the agent of the adding fades, and 「Aに加えてB」 becomes “on top of A, B as well”, expressing accumulation. Since things are piled onto the same item, the two parts are usually of the same kind and direction. And because 「に」 is a case particle, only a noun can precede it, so verbs and adjectives must first be nominalized with 「こと」 or 「の」.

meaning: Responding to someone's expectations or requests, and working to meet them.
connection: Noun + にこたえて・にこたえ・にこたえる + noun (kanji: 「応えて」)

senses.label: Respond to / live up to
senses.meaning: Acting in response to someone's expectations, requests, or wishes, and making them happen. A is usually 「期待」, 「要望」, 「声援」, 「ニーズ」, 「リクエスト」, etc.
senses.connection: Noun + にこたえて／にこたえ、
examples: Responding to the fans' cheers, the player waved.
Living up to my parents' expectations, I became a doctor.
In response to customer requests, we extended our business hours.

senses.label: That meets ...
senses.meaning: 「にこたえる + noun」 modifies a noun: “that meets ...”. The negative potential 「期待にこたえられない」 is also common.
senses.connection: Noun + にこたえる／にこたえた + noun; noun + にこたえられる／にこたえられない
examples: We develop products that meet consumer needs.
I'm sorry I couldn't live up to everyone's expectations.

notes: 「応える」 and 「答える」 are both read 「こたえる」: 「質問に答える」 is answering in words, while 「期待に応える」 is meeting it through action. Writing 「期待に答える」 is generally considered a misuse.
「応える」 and 「応じる」 share a kanji but are read differently: 「要望に応える」 is “to do what the other party wants”, while 「要望に応じる」 is “to agree to a request”. To refuse, say 「ご要望には応じかねます」, not 「応えかねます」.
In business, 「ご要望にお応えして」 and 「ご期待に応えられず、申し訳ございません」 are common. Saying 「要望に応えてあげる」 to a client sounds like you're doing them a favor, which is very rude.

daily.title: At a concert
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about the encore.
daily.example: In response to the encore, they sang one more song for us.

daily.title: A child studying for exams
daily.description: Talking about why a child studies so hard.
daily.example: They study every day, trying to live up to their parents' expectations.

daily.title: Reading sports news
daily.description: A report on a rookie's performance.
daily.example: Rewarding the coach's trust, the rookie scored a goal.

work.title: New product launch
work.description: A company describes a new product in a press release.
work.example: In response to customer feedback, we've released a new size.

work.title: Pledge after promotion
work.description: A promoted employee speaks to their boss.
work.example: I'll do my very best to live up to the company's expectations.

etymology: 「こたえる」 was 「こたふ」 in old Japanese, meaning “to respond, to reply”. Written 「答える」, it means answering in words. Written 「応える」, it means responding to expectations or requests through action. 「〜にこたえて」 uses the latter.

similar.title: 〜に応じて
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; both are written with 「応」 and both have the sense of “responding”. 「に応じて」 means complying with or accepting the other's request, or changing according to circumstances (「収入に応じて」); 「に応えて」 means satisfying the other's expectations and demands through action, with a positive “living up to hopes” feel.

similar.title: 〜に沿って
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; 「ご要望に沿って」 also means doing as the other party wishes. 「に沿って」 stresses not deviating from a policy or wish; 「に応えて」 stresses actively satisfying and fulfilling the other's expectations.

similar.title: 〜に恥じない
similar.explanation: An N1 pattern with a similar meaning, “worthy of ...” (「期待に恥じない成績」); it stresses that the result matches the expectations or reputation. 「に応えて」 stresses taking action in response to expectations.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」 plus the て-form of the verb 「応える（こたえる）」. 「こたえる」 originally means to respond to something coming from the other party; when written 「応える」, what is responded to is not a question but expectations, demands, or support, things “the other party entrusts to you”. So 「Nに応えて」 means “in response to N, ...”, and the way of responding is to satisfy it through action, giving it a positive, “living up to hopes” feel. The first part is always the other's expectation or demand, and the second half is the action you take for it or the result you achieve; 「に応える＋noun」 as a modifier becomes “(products, services) that meet ...”.

meaning: “It's best to ...”, “nothing beats ...”. Usually common-sense advice.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form／い-adj.／な-adj. + に越したことはない

senses.label: It's best to
senses.meaning: Of course ... is best; nothing is better. Usually a common-sense judgment. It often implies “it's not essential” or “if you can't, that's OK”.
senses.connection: Noun／verb dictionary form／い-adj. + に越したことはない (often followed by 「が、〜」)
examples: It never hurts to be careful.
Of course, the healthier your body, the better.
Cheaper rent is always better, but being far from the station is a problem.

senses.label: Polite form and variations
senses.meaning: The polite form is 「〜に越したことはありません」. You can also say 「〜ば、それに越したことはない」: “if ..., that would be ideal”.
senses.connection: 〜に越したことはありません; 〜ば／〜なら + それに越したことはない
examples: It's always best to prepare early.
If you can pass on the first try, that would be ideal.

notes: It means “that would of course be best, but it's not required”, a general common-sense judgment, and is not used for the speaker's strong personal preference: ✕「夏はビールに越したことはない」→○「夏はビールに限る」.
Nouns and な-adjectives attach directly, without 「だ」: ✕「安全だに越したことはない」→○「安全に越したことはない」. Verbs take the dictionary form: ✕「準備したに越したことはない」→○「準備するに越したことはない」.
Saying 「確認するに越したことはありません」 directly to a boss or client sounds preachy. To remind someone, 「念のためご確認いただけますと幸いです」 is more appropriate.

daily.title: Taking an umbrella
daily.description: A family member tells you to take an umbrella.
daily.example: Just in case, it's better to take an umbrella.

daily.title: Talking about checkups
daily.description: Talking about health with a friend.
daily.example: It's best to get a health checkup every year.

daily.title: Choosing a computer
daily.description: Discussing with a friend at an electronics store.
daily.example: A lighter laptop is better, of course, but price matters too.

work.title: Discussing delivery with a supplier
work.description: A buyer explains priorities.
work.example: The sooner the delivery the better, of course, but please put quality first.

work.title: Advice from a senior
work.description: A senior colleague suggests a newcomer get a qualification.
work.example: It never hurts to have a qualification.

etymology: 「越す」 means “to go beyond, to exceed”. 「〜に越したことはない」 literally means “there's nothing that goes beyond ...”, i.e., “... is best”.

similar.title: 〜に限る
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; it also says “... is best”, but it is the speaker's subjective, strong assertion (「疲れた時は寝るに限る」). 「に越したことはない」 is a general common-sense judgment with a milder tone, often with the concession that “if it can't be done, it can't be helped”.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; it is general advice, “you'd better ...”, urging the other person directly (「早く寝たほうがいい」). 「に越したことはない」 stresses “that is of course ideal”, doesn't ask anything of the listener directly, and often takes 「が、〜」.

similar.title: 〜て何よりだ
similar.explanation: An N1 pattern with a similar meaning, also “nothing is better than this”. 「て何よりだ」 expresses relief about a good thing that has already happened (「無事で何よりだ」); 「に越したことはない」 mostly refers to an ideal state that has not yet been realized, or to things in general.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」, the た-form of the verb 「越す」 (“to exceed”), and 「ことはない」. 「Aに越す」 means “to exceed A”; 「越した」 modifies 「こと」, so 「Aに越したことはない」 literally says “there is nothing that exceeds A”, that is, “nothing is better than A”, i.e. “A is best”. Because this is a comparative judgment, “nothing beats it”, and not a demand that “it must be so”, the tone is mild, and it often takes 「が、〜」 to form a concession: “that would of course be best, but ...”.

meaning: “On the occasion of ...”, “when ...”. Used for special or important occasions. Formal and written.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + に際して・に際し・に際しての + noun

senses.label: On the occasion of
senses.meaning: At the time of doing something special, or just before it starts. More formal than 「〜とき」, common in speeches, notices, and official documents. 「に際し」 is more written.
senses.connection: Noun (出発・契約・入学, etc.)／verb dictionary form + に際して／に際し、／に際しては
examples: Before we depart, I'll explain some points to keep in mind.
An ID is required when signing the contract.
When I returned to my home country, I said goodbye to the people who had helped me.

senses.label: Noun modifier: ... at the time of
senses.meaning: 「に際しての + noun」 modifies a noun: “... for/at the time of ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + に際しての + noun
examples: We'd like to inform you about the admission procedures.

notes: Use it only for special, one-time events, not for small things that recur every day: ✕「毎朝の通勤に際して」→○「毎朝通勤するとき」.
Don't mix it up with the connection of 「〜際に」: 「に際して」 takes no 「の」 before it. ✕「出発の際して」→○「出発に際して」 or 「出発の際に」.
「この際」 means “now that we're at it, might as well”, and is not this pattern: 「この際、全部捨ててしまおう」. In speeches and letters, set phrases like 「ご結婚に際し、心よりお祝い申し上げます」 are common.

daily.title: Reading travel info
daily.description: Reading the pre-trip guide from a travel agency.
daily.example: Before traveling, please check your passport's expiration date.

daily.title: Talking about a wedding
daily.description: Telling a friend about getting married.
daily.example: When we got married, we received congratulations from many people.

work.title: Opening speech
work.description: The host speaks at the start of a conference.
work.example: To open this meeting, allow me to say a few words.

work.title: Company rules
work.description: A rule about resignation in the employee handbook.
work.example: When resigning, you must give notice at least one month in advance.

etymology: 「際」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “time, moment” (as in 「この際」, 「実際」). 「〜に際する」 is a formal Chinese-style expression meaning “to come to the time of ...”.

similar.title: 〜にあたって・〜にあたり
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning, and in most cases interchangeable. 「にあたって」 more strongly stresses actively preparing and resolving for an important event about to begin; 「に際して」 more objectively says “right at that time”.

similar.title: 〜際（に）
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are built from 「際」 and the meanings are close. 「〜の際に」 can be used in general situations (「お帰りの際は、忘れ物にご注意ください」); 「に際して」 is used only for special, important matters and is more formal.

similar.title: 〜に先立って
similar.explanation: Both are used at the start of an important matter. 「に先立って」 clearly means “before ... (do something first)”; 「に際して」 means “just at the time of ...”, covering both the moment just before it starts and while it is under way.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」 plus the て-form of the Sino-Japanese する-verb 「際する」. 「際」 originally means “edge, the point where things meet”, extended to “occasion, time”; 「際する」 means “to encounter a certain moment, to come upon the time”. 「Nに際して」 means “just as N arrives”, hence “on the occasion of ...”. The whole construction is a kanbun-style expression, so it is much more formal than 「〜とき」 and is mostly used in speeches and official documents. 「に際し」 is the continuative pause form, more written; 「に際しての＋noun」 turns it into a modifier.

meaning: Before something important, first doing preparation or something else. Formal and written.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + に先立って・に先立ち・に先立つ + noun

senses.label: Prior to
senses.meaning: Before an important event, a preliminary step happens first. The second half is what's done in advance. Common in news, notices, and ceremonies.
senses.connection: Noun (会議・発売・試合, etc.)／verb dictionary form + に先立って／に先立ち、
examples: Prior to the game, an opening ceremony was held.
Ahead of the new product's release, a press conference was held.
Before starting construction, we held a briefing for local residents.

senses.label: Preceding ...
senses.meaning: 「に先立つ + noun」 modifies a noun: “... before ...”, “preceding ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + に先立つ + noun
examples: I was invited to a preview screening before the film's release.

notes: The first part is a formal, important matter, and the second half is preparation for it or an activity held beforehand; used for everyday trifles it sounds exaggerated: ✕「食事に先立って手を洗う」→○「食事の前に手を洗う」.
With a person, 「先立つ」 easily suggests “to die before someone” (「妻に先立たれる」「親に先立つ不孝」). To say you're leaving before someone, don't say 「部長に先立って帰ります」; say 「お先に失礼します」.
「先立つもの」 is an idiom meaning “the thing you need first (money)”: 「旅行したいが、先立つものがない」. It is not this pattern.

daily.title: Reading world news
daily.description: A report on a summit meeting.
daily.example: Ahead of the summit, the two countries' foreign ministers held talks.

daily.title: Watching a live game
daily.description: A commentator describes the pre-game ceremony.
daily.example: Before the start of the match, the national anthem was played.

work.title: Member pre-sale notice
work.description: A notice a company sends to its members.
work.example: Before the general release, we'll hold an advance sale for members.

work.title: Preparing for a meeting
work.description: A secretary emails the attendees.
work.example: Ahead of the meeting, I'll send you the materials.

etymology: 「先立つ」 is 「先（さき）」 + 「立つ」, originally “to stand in front, to go ahead”. It extended to “to come before in time”.

similar.title: 〜まえに
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; both mean “before ...”. 「前に」 is common in both speech and writing and can be used for anything; 「に先立って」 is formal and written, and mostly refers to preparations for an important matter or an event held beforehand.

similar.title: 〜にあたって・〜にあたり
similar.explanation: Both are used at the start of an important matter. 「にあたって」 means “on the occasion of ...”, covers both before and the moment itself, and focuses on “facing this moment”; 「に先立って」 clearly means “before”.

similar.title: 〜に先駆けて
similar.explanation: An N1 pattern with a similar meaning; both contain 「先」. 「に先駆けて」 means “ahead of (others, other places) ...” (「全国に先駆けて導入した」) and stresses getting ahead of others; 「に先立って」 stresses time order.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」 plus the て-form of the verb 「先立つ」. 「先立つ」 is 「先」 (front) plus 「立つ」 (to stand), i.e. “to stand in front”. 「Nに先立って」 literally means “standing ahead of N”, which in terms of time is “before N (done first)”. What stands in front often clears the way for the main event, so the second half is mostly preparation, announcements, or a preliminary ceremony. Using the compound verb 「立つ」 is more formal than simply saying 「前に」, so it appears mostly in news and notices; 「に先立つ＋noun」 can be used as a modifier.

meaning: Imagining someone's feelings or thoughts from their position: “for ..., from ...'s point of view”.
connection: Noun (person・organization) + にしたら／にすれば／にしてみれば

senses.label: From ...'s position
senses.meaning: Guessing how someone (usually another person) feels or sees things from their standpoint. Follows a noun for a person or organization. The second half is usually a guess: 「〜だろう」, 「〜かもしれない」, 「〜はずだ」.
senses.connection: Person noun + にしたら、／にすれば、
examples: For parents, their child's future is probably their biggest worry.
For the shop, rainy days must be a problem because there are fewer customers.
From his point of view, maybe it was just meant as a joke.

senses.label: Putting yourself in their shoes
senses.meaning: 「〜にしてみれば」 and 「〜にしてみたら」 stress “if you put yourself in their shoes”. Often used to show understanding of others.
senses.connection: Person noun + にしてみれば／にしてみたら
examples: From the child's point of view, cram school every day must be tough.
For the other person, I think it was awkward to be turned down so suddenly.

notes: It has the same form as the conditional of the choice-expressing 「〜にする」 but means something completely different: 「コーヒーにしたら？」 means “why not go with coffee?”, while 「子どもにしたら」 means “from the child's point of view”. It is this pattern only when the first part is a person or an organization and the second half guesses their feelings.
The second half mostly takes conjecture such as 「〜だろう」「〜かもしれない」. Making a flat assertion sounds as if you were deciding for someone else: ✕「部長にしたら、この案は反対だ」→○「部長にしたら、この案には反対だろう」.
Saying 「〇〇さんにしたら〜でしょう」 directly to a boss or client may sound like you're second-guessing them. To show consideration, 「〇〇様のお立場からすれば」 is more polite.

daily.title: Getting a friend to see Mom's side
daily.description: Your friend got scolded for coming home late, and you help them see their mom's feelings.
daily.example: Put yourself in your mom's shoes. She was probably too worried to sleep.

daily.title: Noise for the neighbors
daily.description: A family member wants to play piano at night, so you remind them.
daily.example: For the neighbors, piano at night must be noisy.

daily.title: Moving with a pet
daily.description: Talking with family about how a move affects the cat.
daily.example: For a cat, moving is a big stress.

work.title: Customer experience
work.description: A store manager reminds staff in a meeting.
work.example: From the customer's point of view, long waits must be frustrating.

work.title: Being considerate of new hires
work.description: A senior colleague talks about a new employee.
work.example: For a new employee, the first month is all about learning things, so it must be hard.

etymology: Made from the conditional forms 「したら」 and 「すれば」 of 「〜にする」. 「Aにしたら」 originally means “if you set your position as A”, i.e., “if you stand in A's place”.

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; both can be translated “for ...”. 「にとって」 is mostly used for objective evaluation or value judgments, and is often used about yourself too (「私にとって大切な人」); 「にしたら」 stresses putting yourself in someone's shoes to guess their feelings and thoughts.

similar.title: 〜からすると・〜からすれば
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; 「親からすると」 also means looking from someone's standpoint. 「からすると」 can also take the basis of a judgment (「この様子からすると」) and has a wider use; 「にしたら」 attaches only to people or organizations and focuses on guessing their feelings.

similar.title: 〜に言わせれば
similar.explanation: An N1 pattern with a similar meaning: “if you let ... speak” (「父に言わせれば、最近の若者は甘い」), where the second half is that person's own view or evaluation. In 「にしたら」 the second half is mostly a guess at their feelings.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」 plus the conditional forms 「したら」 and 「すれば」 of the verb 「する」. 「Nにする」 means “to settle on N”, so 「Nにしたら」 literally says “if (the standpoint) were settled as N”, i.e. “if you stood in N's position”. Since you imagine standing in another person's place, the second half naturally conjectures how that person thinks or feels, so it often takes 「〜だろう」. 「〜にしてみれば」 adds 「みる」 (“to try”), i.e. “try standing in N's position and looking”, which strengthens the sense of putting yourself in their shoes.

meaning: A concession: “even if ...”, “whatever ...”. More written than 「にしても」.
connection: Noun／verb・adjective plain form + にしろ・にせよ (nouns and な-adjectives can also take 「であるにせよ」)

senses.label: Even if
senses.meaning: Even if A is accepted (as fact or hypothesis), the judgment in B doesn't change. The second half is usually the speaker's opinion, evaluation, or demand, such as 「〜べきだ」 or 「〜てはいけない」.
senses.connection: Verb・い-adj. plain form／noun + にしろ／にせよ (often with 「たとえ」 or 「どんな」)
examples: Even if you're busy, you should at least get in touch.
Whatever the reason, violence is unacceptable.
Even as a joke, you shouldn't say something like that.

senses.label: Set phrases: anyway
senses.meaning: 「いずれにせよ」, 「いずれにしろ」, 「何にせよ」, and 「どちらにしろ」 are set phrases meaning “anyway, in any case”.
senses.connection: いずれ／何／どちら + にしろ／にせよ、
examples: In any case, we have to reach a conclusion by tomorrow.
Anyway, I'm glad you're safe.

notes: 「〜にしろ」 on its own is simply the imperative of 「する」: 「静かにしろ！」 (“Be quiet!”) and 「好きにしろ」 (“Do as you like”) are very blunt commands. To make a concession with a な-adjective, use 「好きであるにせよ」 or 「好きだとしても」, so it won't be heard as a command.

The second half is the speaker's judgment, claim or demand, saying that “whatever the first part, the conclusion stays”. It can't be used when the second half merely states a fact: ✕「忙しいにせよ、連絡できなかった」→○「忙しいにせよ、連絡ぐらいはするべきだった」.
「いずれにしろ」 is rather colloquial. To a boss or client, or in business email, 「いずれにしましても」 or 「いずれにせよ」 is more appropriate.

daily.title: Telling a friend to reply
daily.description: Your friend doesn't want to go to a party, so you remind them.
daily.example: Even if you're not going, you'd better reply.

daily.title: Reading an editorial
daily.description: A newspaper editorial gives the writer's view.
daily.example: Whatever the circumstances, rules should be followed.

daily.title: Talking about saving
daily.description: Talking about money with family.
daily.example: Even if it's just a little, it's better to save some money.

work.title: Wrapping up a meeting
work.description: The chair sums up the discussion.
work.example: In any case, let's decide on a direction by next week.

work.title: Replying to a client email
work.description: Explaining delivery progress to a client.
work.example: Even if there's a slight delay, we'll definitely meet the deadline.

etymology: 「しろ」 and 「せよ」 are both imperative forms of 「する」 (「せよ」 is the classical imperative and more written). 「Nにしろ」 literally means “let it be N”. From “granting it for now”, it became a concession: “even if ...”.

similar.title: 〜にしても
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are built from 「に＋する」 and mean the same. 「にしても」 can be used in speech and writing and sounds softer; 「にしろ」 and 「にせよ」 are more written and stiffer, and 「にせよ」 is the most formal.

similar.title: 〜としても
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; it stresses “even supposing ...” and is mostly used for hypothetical conditions (「たとえ失敗したとしても」). 「にしろ」 can either acknowledge an existing fact or be used for a hypothesis.

similar.title: 〜であれ／〜であれ〜であれ
similar.explanation: An N1 pattern with a similar meaning; written, it attaches mainly to nouns or question words (「どんな理由であれ」). 「にしろ」 and 「にせよ」 can also take the plain form of verbs and adjectives, so their range is wider.

similar.title: 〜にしろ〜にしろ・〜にしても〜にしても
similar.explanation: Same origin; it is this pattern repeated twice. 「にしろ」 gives one case and means “even if ...”; 「〜にしろ〜にしろ」 gives two cases and means “whichever it is ...”.

formation: Built from the case particle 「に」 plus the imperative 「しろ」 (spoken) or 「せよ」 (literary) of 「する」. 「Nにしろ」 literally means “let's just take it as N”: the speaker provisionally accepts the first part, “even if it is N”, then turns and states a conclusion that doesn't change, forming the concession “even if ..., still ...”. The imperative here isn't ordering anyone; it carries the tone of “let's just say so” with a leave-it-be attitude; 「せよ」 is a literary imperative, so 「にせよ」 is more written. Question word ＋ 「にせよ」 (「何にせよ」「いずれにせよ」) provisionally accepts all possibilities, which becomes “anyway, in any case”.

meaning: Lists two (often opposite) cases: “whether A or B, either way ...”.
connection: Noun／verb・adjective plain form + にしろ + noun／plain form + にしろ (also 「にせよ〜にせよ」, 「にしても〜にしても」)

senses.label: Whether A or B
senses.meaning: Lists two opposite cases (such as doing or not doing): B holds either way. The second half is usually the speaker's judgment or request.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + にしろ + verb nai-form + にしろ
examples: Whether you go or not, please let us know early.
Whether you agree or disagree, you should state your reasons clearly.
Whether you buy it or not, it's worth having a look first.

senses.label: Listing similar things
senses.meaning: Lists two things of the same kind as examples: “whether it's A or B, it's the same”.
senses.connection: Noun + にしろ + noun + にしろ
examples: Whether it's meat or fish, choosing fresh ones is important.
Whether it's Japanese or English, daily practice is essential for learning a language.

notes: The second half is a judgment, claim or demand, and doesn't take a plain past fact: ✕「行くにしろ行かないにしろ、彼は来た」→○「行くにしろ行かないにしろ、連絡はしてほしい」.
The two items must be opposite poles (do / don't, agree / oppose) or representatives of the same kind (meat / fish); two unrelated items can't be paired: ✕「雨にしろ映画にしろ」.

When the same verb is set against itself, the second item takes the negative, and the repeated part can be omitted: 「採用するにせよしないにせよ」. Leaving out the negative makes it a redundant repeat that makes no sense.
「にしたって〜にしたって」 is very casual; in formal documents and business, use 「にせよ〜にせよ」.

daily.title: Deciding what to eat
daily.description: Choosing a restaurant with family on the weekend.
daily.example: Whether it's Japanese or Western food, I want something tasty today.

daily.title: Advising a friend
daily.description: A friend can't decide what to do after graduation.
daily.example: Whether you study abroad or get a job, think it through before you decide.

work.title: Hiring process
work.description: An HR manager gives instructions.
work.example: Whether we hire them or not, inform the candidate of the result.

work.title: Internal notice
work.description: Explaining training attendance requirements.
work.example: Whether full-time or part-time, attending the training is mandatory.

etymology: Made by repeating the concessive 「にしろ」, 「にせよ」, or 「にしても」 twice. 「しろ」 and 「せよ」 are imperative forms of 「する」. 「Aにしろ、Bにしろ」 literally means “let it be A, let it be B”: both cases are granted, and the conclusion stays the same.

similar.title: 〜にしろ・〜にせよ
similar.explanation: Same origin; this pattern is its repeated form. 「にしろ」 gives one case and means “even if ...”; 「〜にしろ〜にしろ」 gives two cases and means “whichever it is ...”.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うが〜まいが／〜(よ)うと〜まいと
similar.explanation: An N1 pattern with a similar meaning: 「行こうが行くまいが」 means the same as 「行くにしろ行かないにしろ」. It uses the volitional form, is stronger, and carries a “do as you like, it doesn't matter” attitude, with 「自由だ」「関係ない」 often in the second half.

similar.title: 〜であれ／〜であれ〜であれ
similar.explanation: An N1 written pattern with a similar meaning, attaching mainly to nouns (「大人であれ子どもであれ」); 「にしろ〜にしろ」 can also take verbs, so it has wider use.

similar.title: 〜でも〜でも
similar.explanation: A colloquial pattern with a similar meaning, attaching mainly to nouns (「肉でも魚でも」); 「にしろ〜にしろ」 is more written and can also take verbs to mean “whether you do it or not”.

formation: Built by repeating the concessive 「にしろ」 (「に」 plus the imperative of 「する」) twice. A single 「Aにしろ」 means “let's just take it as A”; accepting both A and B in this way says that the conclusion is unchanged in either case, giving “whether A or B, ...”. The two items are usually opposite poles (do / don't do) or representatives of the same kind (meat / fish): the two ends cover every possibility, and that is what makes the conclusion sound valid “either way”. 「にせよ〜にせよ」 and 「にしても〜にしても」 are built the same way and differ only in register.
